# Efficient Reasoning for Large Reasoning Language Models via Certainty-Guided Reflection Suppression

- **Authors**: Jiameng Huang, Baijiong Lin, Guhao Feng, Jierun Chen, Di He, Lu Hou
- **Venue**: AAAI
- **Published**: 2026-01-01
- **Source**: local
- **Topics**: overthinking

## In one line

CGRS is a training-free, decoding-time method that suppresses reflection-trigger tokens (e.g. "Wait", "But") probabilistically, in proportion to a token-entropy-based certainty score computed at checkpoint probes, cutting reasoning length by 18.5-41.9% with little to no accuracy loss.

## Problem

Large reasoning language models generate reflection behaviors (backtracking, re-verification), signaled by trigger words like "Wait", "Alternatively", "But", "Hmm", even after reaching a correct intermediate answer. This overthinking inflates token usage and inference cost, and existing training-free fixes either follow a fixed prompt budget (insensitive to per-instance need) or use hard-coded early-exit conditions tied to the end-of-think token (which fails on models like QwQ-32B that keep reflecting past that marker).

## Contributions

- Proposes CGRS, a training-free, model-agnostic, decoding-time method that suppresses reflection-trigger tokens based on the model's own internal certainty signals rather than a fixed schedule or hard-coded exit condition.
- Introduces a certainty estimation mechanism based on entropy of tentative probed answers at reasoning checkpoints, plus a suppression rule that only intervenes when certainty exceeds a threshold.
- Shows the method achieves 18.5-41.9% token reduction with accuracy comparable to (or occasionally above) the unmodified model, across 7 model checkpoints (4B-32B) and 4 benchmarks, outperforming TALE, NoThinking, Dynasor and DEER on the accuracy/length tradeoff, including on QwQ-32B where end-of-think-based early-exit baselines largely fail because that model keeps reflecting past the </think> token.

## Method

CGRS operates in two phases at inference time, with no retraining. (1) Certainty estimation: at structural checkpoints (marked by \n\n in the generated text), the model is probed with an appended prompt ("**Final Answer: \boxed") to elicit a tentative answer a, generated by a separate concurrent decode that does not alter the main trajectory. The certainty score C = 1 - (mean per-token entropy of the probed answer tokens / log|V|), bounded to [0,1] by the max-entropy normalizer log|V| (V = vocabulary); lower entropy in the tentative answer means higher C. (2) Dynamic reflection-trigger suppression: a suppression probability p = max(0, (C-delta)/(1-delta)) is computed from C against a threshold delta (set to 0.9 in the main experiments). With probability p at each checkpoint, the logits of a pre-identified set of reflection-trigger tokens (variants of "Wait", "But", "Alternatively", "Hmm", collected via tokenizer frequency analysis, listed in Appendix Table 3) are set to a large negative value before sampling the next token, blocking the model from emitting that trigger and thus from opening a new reflection cycle. Suppression only occurs when C > delta, so low-confidence steps are left untouched and can still self-correct.

## Results

Table 1 (per-model AVG columns across AIME24/AMC23/MATH500/GPQA-D, CGRS row vs Vanilla row): Qwen3-4B Acc 72.5% (Vanilla 74.5%), length reduction (LR) 38.1%; Qwen3-8B Acc 75.9% (Vanilla 77.2%), LR 29.3%; Qwen3-14B Acc 80.8% (Vanilla 80.1%, i.e. CGRS slightly higher), LR 25.4%; Qwen3-32B Acc 79.2% (Vanilla 82.2%), LR 31.2%; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B Acc 65.2% (Vanilla 66.8%), LR 41.9%; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B Acc 64.7% (Vanilla 61.7%, CGRS higher), LR 18.5%; QwQ-32B Acc 80.8% (Vanilla 80.2%, CGRS higher), LR 30.5%. Overall the paper's headline claim (Fig. 1 caption, Abstract) is an average token reduction of 18.5-41.9% while preserving accuracy. Table 2 (AMC23, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, comparing certainty-guided suppression to fixed suppression probabilities): p=0 (Vanilla) Acc 87.5%, Len 5861 tokens; p=0.25 Acc 81.7%, Len 3729; p=0.5 Acc 80.0%, Len 3266; p=1.0 Acc 76.7%, Len 2373; Certainty-Guided (Eq. 2, i.e. CGRS) Acc 88.3%, Len 3406 -- CGRS reduces length by 41.9% versus Vanilla while accuracy is slightly higher (88.3% vs 87.5%), whereas all fixed-p baselines reduce length less while also losing accuracy. Table 4 (threshold ablation, AMC23, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B): delta=0.9 gives Acc 88.3%, LR 41.9%; delta=0.5 gives Acc 76.2%, LR 48.5%; delta=0.1 gives Acc 72.5%, LR 53.7% -- lowering the threshold trades accuracy for more length reduction.

## Limitations

The paper does not report a stated limitations section. Baselines TALE, NoThinking, Dynasor and DEER are re-run by the authors rather than copied from other papers (Table 1 caption describes them as directly compared under the same protocol), so this is not a case of borrowed baseline numbers. The method requires an extra concurrent probing decode at every \n\n checkpoint, adding inference-time overhead not quantified in wall-clock or FLOPs terms in the main text. The threshold delta is fixed per experiment (0.9) and Table 4 shows results are sensitive to its choice, without a principled way to set it per model/task. Reflection-trigger token sets are hand-curated per tokenizer (Qwen2Tokenizer, LlamaTokenizerFast; Appendix Table 3), so extending to a new model family requires redoing that enumeration.

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: CGRS suppresses reflection at the token-generation level using a certainty score computed from the entropy of a probed tentative answer at \n\n checkpoints, and applies suppression probabilistically (p scaling with how far certainty exceeds a threshold delta) rather than deterministically. This places it between NEAT, which also suppresses reflection-token logits but as a graded intermediate action driven by exit-associated neuron activations rather than a probed-answer entropy signal, and NoWait, which masks reflective tokens outright regardless of confidence and is reported elsewhere to hurt hard tasks; CGRS's probabilistic, certainty-gated suppression is explicitly evaluated against fixed suppression probabilities (Table 2) and shown to preserve accuracy better than always-suppress (p=1, equivalent to a NoWait-like hard mask) or any fixed intermediate p. It also differs from RCP/RCPD and ThinkBrake, which key off the rank or log-probability margin of the literal </think> token: CGRS instead probes for a full tentative final answer and measures entropy over it, which the authors argue lets it work on models like QwQ-32B that keep reflecting past </think>, where end-of-think-anchored baselines (including DEER, which also uses a single-step confidence check at transition cues like "Wait") largely fail to compress.

## Abstract

Recent Large Reasoning Language Models (LRLMs) employ long chain-of-thought reasoning with complex reflection behaviors, typically signaled by specific trigger words (e.g., "Wait" and "Alternatively"), to enhance performance. However, these reflection behaviors can lead to the overthinking problem where the generation of redundant reasoning steps that unnecessarily increase token usage, raise inference costs, and reduce practical utility. In this paper, we propose Certainty-Guided Reflection Suppression (CGRS), a novel method that mitigates overthinking in LRLMs while maintaining reasoning accuracy. CGRS operates by dynamically suppressing the model's generation of reflection triggers when it exhibits high confidence in its current response, thereby preventing redundant reflection cycles without compromising output quality. Our approach is model-agnostic, requires no retraining or architectural modifications, and can be integrated seamlessly with existing autoregressive generation pipelines. Extensive experiments across four reasoning benchmarks (i.e., AIME24, AMC23, MATH500, and GPQA-D) demonstrate CGRS's effectiveness: it reduces token usage by an average of 18.5% to 41.9% while preserving accuracy and also achieves the optimal balance between length reduction and performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines. These results hold consistently across model architectures (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill series, QwQ-32B, and Qwen3 family), and scales (4B to 32B parameters), highlighting CGRS's practical value for efficient reasoning.
